content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an approach to improve the Deep Image Prior (DIP) in terms of computational efficiency by leveraging the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH). The proposed approach is shown to be capable of reducing the number of parameters in DIP (hence saving reconstruction time) by a significant factor while still preserving the performance (image quality) of the original DIP. Transferability of the proposed LTH-DIP is also demonstrated across images and restoration task types.

content.title: Response to Reviewer fDwJ
content.comment:
Q1: Some details of the proposed approach are not mentioned or clarified. Which task is used for the test in Fig. 3? This should be noted in the caption. 

[A]: Thanks for pointing out, we have added the background task denoising to the Figure 3 caption.

Q2: In Fig. 5, are the transferred LIP winning tickets obtained using single-IMP or multi-IMP? is the test image used in finding the transferred LIP winning tickets? 

[A]: We are sorry to be unclear about the settings here and thank you for pointing it out. In Fig. 5, the transferred LIP winning tickets are obtained by multi-IMP via training on the set5 dataset (*baby.png*, *woman.png*, *head.png*, *bird.png* and *butterfly.png*). And we evaluate the subnetworks on those images and images from other domains (e.g., *F16.png*, *zebra.png*, *baboon.png* and *pepper.png* in Fig. 5, which are **unseen** during finding the winning tickets). We have added the relevant descriptions in Fig. 5 captions.

Q3: How is the mask mu' created (the sparsity of mu' is not updated in each iteration)? The objective function for training is not given. How is the j determined? Is the algorithm intended to only find the desired subnet or it also gives the final restored image?

[A]: The mask $\ mu^\prime$ is updated in every pruning iteration (not optimization iterations of the DIP model). In single-image based IMP, the objective function is exactly the one used in DIP models. In this paper, we define j as 3,000 for DIP optimizations (this iteration number is recommended by [1]). The pruning process can be viewed as an iterative process:
* Randomly initialize the dense DIP model;
* Optimize the network for iterations;
* Prune 20% of parameters (L1 unstructured pruning), and create the mask;
* Reset the remaining parameters to initializations and apply the mask to the structure.

Our goal is to obtain the sparse mask of the DIP network structure. Once we get the mask in desired sparsity, we indeed can construct one very sparse network architecture for DIP on one image, and then always reuse the constructed one for the future optimization of DIP with new input images (probably for another restoration task). And the high sparsity in that constructed network leads to sparse training in DIP and greatly saves flops (assuming the same number of training epochs), besides memory.

[1] NAS-DIP: Learning Deep Image Prior with Neural Architecture Search, ECCV 2020.

Q4: Some statements in the paper are incorrect in section 4.

[A]: We are sorry to cause confusion. We have toned down and modified this part as “results presented in Fig. 4 show that multi-image LIP subnetworks can achieve better performances than dense DIP models and randomly pruned ones in the cross-domain setting.”

Q5: The single-IMP might also have this transferability though not as strong. A comparison is necessary.

[A]: We have added a comparison experiment in Fig.14 in Appendix B. We evaluate several single-image based LIP subnetworks (Baby-LIP, Bird-LIP, Woman-LIP and Butterfly-LIP) on the *Baby.png* and compare their performances with MUlti-LIP subnetworks. The experimental results are summarized in Fig.14. We found that when the sparsity level is low (0%-40%), the single-LIP subnetworks perform a little worse than the LIPs obtained on *Baby.png*. When the sparsity level increases (e.g., the number of remaining parameters is less than 0.6 million), they usually tend to perform comparably. Another intriguing phenomenon is that Multi-LIP performs comparably with the LIPs obtained on *Baby.png* but can perform better than the other LIPs when the sparsity level is high, which also demonstrates that Multi-LIP could have better transferability than single-image based LIP subnetworks.

Q6: Image classification requires training on the massive datasets and is thus not relevant to the DIP (untrained networks) topic.

We respectfully disagree. We studied the performance of LIP subnetworks on image classification to see whether they can transfer from low-level computer vision tasks to high-level ones. This is also one of our contributions to LTH community:  since it is uncertain whether high-sparsity DNN is still viable for low-level vision tasks such as DIPs, we find that the LIP matching subnetworks cannot directly transfer to high-level vision tasks such as classification.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tried to improve deep image prior (DIP), by exploring the ``lottery ticket'' property of deep neural networks (DNNs). The proposed method is called lottery image prior (LIP). The main assumption behind LIP is the so-called lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH), i.e., for an over-parameterized DNN, there could be a sparse subnetwork having a comparable performance. The authors integrated LTH to DIP, and obtained the LIP by pruning. Experiments, with several image processing tasks, have been conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
* The motivation of this work is reasonable and interesting.
* The authors have done extensive experiments with detailed analyses.

### Weaknesses
* It seems that when applying LIP, the learning process will contain pruning in addition to parameter update, which makes the whole process more complicated.
* I do not quite understand the transfer property. Does that mean fix the network structure learned by current image(s), and then only learn the parameters for a new image to-be-processed? If so, why do not using random structure? I know that the authors claimed that uniform randomness leads to inferior performance, but if a proper random strategy is specified, the performance can compete with that by transfer.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity

The method is clearly presented. However, the writing seems not be an ordinary paper. Specifically, the Introduction part is somewhat like a response to reviewers, while not a normal one.

### Quality

The overall quality of this paper is good, despite the weaknesses mentioned above.

### Novelty

The novelty relatively limited, but the work is still significant. Specifically, though applying LTH to DIP is straightforward, make it really work could be nontrivial.

### Reproducibility

The implementation details provided in the paper, including both the main text and appendices, are limited, and thus I do not think it is easy to reproduce the results. The authors promise to release code upon acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This manuscript studies a problem to prune the over-parameterized deep image prior (DIP) model in order to find a better DIP which is more sparse while still keeps similar performance, that is, to find a “intermediate” parameterized image priors that achieve better trade-offs between performance and efficiency.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ This paper studies an interesting problem how many parameters may be sufficient to obtain good performance in DIP models, based on the over-parameterization nature of DIP model.

Weakness / Questions:
- Motivation is not clear. After reading the whole paper, my understanding is that this paper aims at proposing a method to prune the DIP models in order to find a sparser DIP model with comparable performance. But in the introduction, this motivation seems not to be very clear. Is efficiency the key target for this work? How could this be reflected from what applications? For DIP-based methods for inverse problem solving, they are usually single-image restoration and reconstruction. How would efficiency be a key factor or motivation in these tasks or applications? These questions may not be covered well from the current introduction. 

- Summary of contribution is not concise and may raise confusion. In Sec. 1.1, the author uses a quite detailed long list to state the contributions of this paper, but this may make the key contribution of the work unclear to the readers. Moreover, some claims may need to be more precise and careful. For example, the author claims “we propose a continuous “interpolation” between over-parameterized and under-parameterized image priors”. How to define the “interpolation” between these two kinds of image priors? Is that on model structure, performance, or parameter numbers? Does there exist some continuous manifold to describe the connections between these models? Besides, the author claims “Beyond “matching”, our found LIP subnetworks can even outperform DIP models on several image restoration tasks (shown in Figure 2)”. Although Figure 2 demonstrates some result examples with similar performance from full model and sparsity, the quantitative and qualitative results difference is quite minor and almost comparable. 

- Methodology novelty. Section 3.2 describes the main pruning method used in this work, which mainly follows the iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) method. Beyond applying this to DIP with single or multiple images, what is the method novelty proposed in this work? How does the LTH guide the algorithm design?

- Stronger baselines for experimental comparison. In order to support the effectiveness of the proposed pruning method for DIP model, the paper compares with some baseline methods including Random Prune and SNIP (Lee et al., 2018) prune methods. It may be better to compare with stronger baselines to make the results more convincing such as the recent SOTA pruning methods.


- Writings and organizations:
Algorithms 1 and 2 may be better to be in the main text, which is an important part for the reader to understand the pruning methodology. In Algorithm 1 and 2, is it better to clearly state how the new mask is created in step 2, which may also be one of the key steps in this pruning algorithm?

content.title: Response to Reviewer bXEi
content.comment:
Q1: Motivation is not clear. Is efficiency the key target for this work? 

[A]: 1. We are afraid there exists a misunderstanding regarding our work. Efficiency is definitely not the key target or motivation. Our key target instead is to verify the existence of a "compact" DIP model that is free from severe overfitting but at the same time different from the deep decoder. We want it partially because the deep decoder is bad in terms of performance (e.g., inpainting and super-resolution).

2. Efficiency is a natural byproduct that results from pruning and sparsity. Improving efficiency could reduce the single-image inference time of DIP to accelerate restoration and reconstruction, which could be helpful in latency-sensitive applications.

3. We have clarified the above points in the introduction of the revised version.

Q2: Summary of contribution is not concise and may raise confusion.

[A]: We are sorry to cause confusion. We will modify claims in section 1.1 as follows: In between over- and under-parameterized image prior models, we aim to use sparsity to find an intermediate parameterized network. Also, we have modified and toned down throughout the paper: our found matching LIP subnetworks can achieve comparable performances with high sparsities and have powerful transferability across different images and restoration tasks.

Q3: Methodology novelty. 

[A]: We proposed 2 algorithms in the paper: single-image based IMP and weight-sharing IMP. Compared with previous LTH methods: 

* Until now, LTH has not been demonstrated for image inverse problems or DNN-based priors, to our best knowledge. Most LTH works studied discriminative tasks, with few exceptions (Chen et al., 2021d). It is therefore uncertain whether high-sparsity DNN is still viable for low-level vision tasks such as DIPs.

* Existing LTH works typically require a training set to locate the sparse subnetwork. In contrast, owing to the nature of DIP, we train a DNN to overfit one specific image. While a handful of papers studied LTH in “data diet” settings (Chen et al., 2021a; Paul et al., 2022), this paper pushes the extreme to “one-shot lottery ticket finding” for the first time. We also develop a multi-image variant of LIP which boosts performance in cross-domain fitting.

* DIP fitting practically relies on early-stopping to avoid overfitting noise in images. The same risk exists in our iterative pruning, and we demonstrate how to robustly find the sparse matching subnetwork from one noisy image, without needing a clean reference image.

We are not claiming "finding a new pruning method" as our technical contribution. Our discovery is to find the compact DIP models in a different but more beneficial (two-fold as we discussed in the introduction) way compared to the deep decoder. Pruning is just our tool here.

Q4: Stronger baselines for experimental comparison.

[A]: Thanks for your suggestions. We further compare the LIP subnetworks with the “SynFlow” [a], one of the STOA pruning-at-initialization methods, in Table.4 in Appendix B. We observed that SynFlow subnetworks achieve comparable performances with the dense network and LIPs when at low sparsity levels (e.g., from 0% to 20%.). But LIP subnetworks start to win them out when the sparsity level increases (e.g., from 60% to 90%.). Also, the LIPs can achieve comparable performances when at extreme sparsities (e.g., when the sparsity level equals 80%.). But the “SynFlow” subnetworks have already failed. 

Also, one paper [b] has demonstrated that several so-called “advanced” pruning methods are no significantly better than magnitude-based pruning, and IMP prevails over them all. Our experimental results also act as side support to this paper.

[a] "Pruning neural networks without any data by iteratively conserving synaptic flow." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 6377-6389.

[b] “Pruning Neural Networks at Initialization: Why Are We Missing the Mark?”, ICLR 2021.

Q5: Writings and organizations: Algorithms 1 and 2 may be better to be in the main text. Better clarify how the new mask is created.

[A]: Thanks for pointing this out. We have moved Algorithm 1,2 to section 3. We have also added the relevant descriptions of mask creations in Appendix A “MORE DISCUSSIONS OF THE EXPERIMENTS” - “Definition of Subnetworks and Finding Them”.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work explores the parametrization for Deep Image Prior in various inverse problems by leveraging the lottery ticket hypothesis, which is a method to prune a trained deep neural network while maintaining its performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Exploring a good network structure for deep image prior, which led to improved performance, is novel.

Weakness:
- It is unclear if the proposed method is practical. In principle, the network should be trained first with full parameters for deep image prior and then it will be optimized using the lottery ticket hypothesis. It was making sense for the problems with large-scale training data (since it will be used for testing with good, robust performance), but deep image prior has no training, so this procedure should happen for every inference. Of course, its structure can be found for one image and then it can be applied to another image, but it is unclear how much performance gap is there between these two cases.
- This work explores the sparsity in network. It may remove the necessity for choosing the number of iterations in the original deep image prior, but it introduces a new hyper-parameter, the level of sparsity. It is apparent that this is also an important parameter for optimal performance as shown in this work. Robustness to this sparsity level seems important for the proposed method useful. It will be interesting to show the results of using one image for pruning and then another image for re-training.
- One major concern is that the results over increasing sparsity levels are not really consistently changing. For example, Figure 8 shows different images with increasing sparsity levels, but it is not easy to see any trend on image changes. This is somewhat different from the sparsity in any transformations (e.g., sparse representations in wavelet domain - degradation is happening gradually with increasing sparsity).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- There are a number of prior works on deep image prior with an external regularizer. Another way of enforcing the sparsity is using a regularizer such as TV (e.g., J Liu et al., Image restoration using total variation regularized deep image prior, IEEE ICASSP 2019). These may be computationally more appealing than the proposed method.
- There are also a number of works on designing losses for deep image prior so that the network will not be overfitted. For example, see the following work: Y Jo et al., Rethinking deep image prior for denoising, ICCV 2021.
content.summary_of_the_review: While I appreciate the idea of the proposed method, the proposed method does not look practical due to massive computation (over the original deep image prior or other pre-trained methods) and newly introduced hyper-parameter that seems sensitive to performance. Moreover, the proposed method does not seem to be well-understood in terms of different sparsity levels. Thus, in its current form, it is hard to recommend its acceptance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer eUHy
content.comment:
Q1: Since DIP has no training, it is unclear if the proposed method is practical. Its structure can be found for one image and then it can be applied to another image, but it is unclear how much performance gap is there between these two cases.

[A]: Thank you for the question. First and foremost, we would like to clarify that the original DIP model does have the training phase, that is, overfitting the model parameters at one degraded image. Therefore, we can naturally apply iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) to the DIP model. To be specific, during the IMP loop, we first train the DIP models for 3000 iterations and then generate the sparse masks by pruning a fixed ratio (20% for example) of the remaining parameters with small magnitudes (as described in Algorithm 1,2 and [a]). Then we reset the remaining parameters to their initial values, preserve the current pruning mask and repeat the optimization-and-pruning process for several iterations until we reach our desired sparsity ratio. Finally, we will obtain the mask and can construct the sparse subnetworks (add the mask to the dense model, without hurting the original network structure).

[a] Frankle Jonathan and Michael Carbin. "The lottery ticket hypothesis: Finding sparse, trainable neural networks.", ICLR 2019.

Secondly, despite the computational efficiency during *inference* brought by sparsity, it is the transferability that makes our method more practically useful. As we have empirically proved, our identified sparse subnetworks can restore different images and work in different inverse problems. We summarized the two observations here (which you can find in Section 4 “LIP in Untrained Image Priors”):
LIP can transfer across images. As we obtained the multi-image LIPs from Set5, we evaluate them on different images in Fig.4. For instance, Fig. 4(a) shows the evaluation results on *F16.png* and we found the multi LIPs perform comparably well (better at extreme sparsities) with LIP dedicatedly found on the *F16.png* (the same phenomenon is reflected on the *face-4.png* (Fig.4(c)) and *face-2.png* (Fig.4(d))). This shows that LIP has reasonable transferability across images, even for those coming from slightly different domains.
LIP can transfer across image restoration tasks. We first find three LIPs for the denoising, inpainting and super-resolution tasks respectively and then transfer between them, as shown in Fig. 5. We observe that a LIP winning ticket transferred from another image restoration task always yields restoration performance comparable with the single-image LIP found on the original task, sometimes even better, for example in Fig. 5(a) and 5(g). This transferability means that we indeed can construct one very sparse network architecture for DIP on one image, and then always reuse the constructed one for the future optimization of DIP with new input images (probably for another restoration task). And the high sparsity in that constructed network leads to sparse training in DIP and greatly saves flops (assuming the same number of training epochs), besides memory.

As for the performance gap, it is similar to the settings of transferability experiments — we compare the performance of (1) LIPs obtained from other images with that of (2) LIPs obtained dedicatedly from this single image. We have added a comparison experiment in Fig.14 in Appendix B. We evaluate several single-image based LIP subnetworks (Baby-LIP, Bird-LIP, Woman-LIP and Butterfly-LIP) on the *Baby.png* and compare their performances with MUlti-LIP subnetworks. The experimental results are summarized in Fig.14. We found that when the sparsity level is low (0%-40%), the single-LIP subnetworks perform a little worse than the LIPs obtained on *Baby.png*. When the sparsity level increases (e.g., the number of remaining parameters is less than 0.6 million), they usually tend to perform comparably well. Another intriguing phenomenon is that Multi-LIP performs comparably with the LIPs obtained on *Baby.png* but can perform better than the other LIPs when the sparsity level is high, which also demonstrates that Multi-LIP could have better transferability than single-image based LIP subnetworks.

content.title: Response to Reviewer eUHy (part II)
content.comment:
Q2: It is apparent that the sparsity level is an important parameter for optimal performance. It will be interesting to show the results of using one image for pruning and then another image for re-training.

[A]: As we mentioned in our response to your first question, when applying the IMP to DIP model, the sparsity level will also increase gradually along the iterations of IMP (not the training iterations of DIP). For example, if we set the pruning rate to 20% in each iteration of IMP (prune 20% parameters every iteration), then the sequence of LIP models will have sparsity levels of 0% (dense models), 20% (1st iteration), 36% (2nd iteration), 48.8% (3rd iteration) and so on. Formally, if the pruning rate is p, then the sparsity level of the n-th iteration will be 1-(1-p)^n. Therefore, we can easily control the final sparsity levels of LIP models by stopping after certain IMP iterations where we have reached desired sparsity levels.

Also, we discussed how to robustly stop the IMP to find the optimal subnetwork in Appendix B “Ablation Study of LIP Subnetworks” - “Discussions about the ‘early-stopping’ in the single-image based IMP loops”. The key point is to observe the tendency of training losses in each IMP iterations. If the losses increase consecutively for a number of IMP iterations, it means that the model capacity has become insufficient for DIP fitting and thus we should stop pruning. This heuristic is easy to implement and does not require access to the ground truth images, and is found to work well empirically as shown in Fig. 13 in Appendix B in the updated manuscript.

As for your request of “showing the results of using one image for pruning and then another image for re-training”, this is also similar to our newly added experiments in Fig.13 in Appendix B. We evaluate several single-image based LIP subnetworks (Baby-LIP, Bird-LIP, Woman-LIP and Butterfly-LIP) on the *Baby.png* and compare their performances with MUlti-LIP subnetworks. The experimental results are summarized in Fig.13. We found that when the sparsity level is low (0%-40%), the single-LIP subnetworks perform a little worse than the LIPs obtained on *Baby.png*. When the sparsity level increases (e.g., the number of remaining parameters is less than 0.6 million), they usually tend to perform comparably well.

Q3: One major concern is that the results over increasing sparsity levels are not really consistently changing (Figure 8).

[A]: There may exist a misunderstanding. We evaluated the effectiveness of LIP subnetworks in GAN on the testset of CelebA-HQ and we did observe the following phenomenon: as the sparsity of the model increases, the quality of the face images inferred by the model gradually decreases (e.g., the ears and hair will be blurred, and the lips and nose will appear distorted.). But we can find a small number of high-quality face-generation images despite the high sparsity. This phenomenon has been previously proved by [1].

[1]: Xuxi Chen, Zhenyu Zhang, Yongduo Sui, and Tianlong Chen. Gans can Play Lottery Tickets too. ICLR 2021.

Q4: There are a number of prior works on deep image prior with an external regularizer (e.g., J Liu et al., Image restoration using total variation regularized deep image prior, IEEE ICASSP 2019).

[A]: Thank you for bringing up these interesting works and we have added them to section 2.1 “Over-parameterized Image Priors”. As we mentioned in Q1, computational savings lie in the transferability of found LIP subnetworks. This transferability (across different images & tasks) means that we indeed can construct one very sparse network architecture for DIP on one image, and then always reuse the constructed one for the future optimization of DIP with new input images (probably for another restoration task). And the high sparsity in that constructed network leads to sparse training in DIP and greatly saves flops (assuming the same number of training epochs), besides memory. Also, we notice that their proposed models usually achieve PSNR values 0.5dB higher than the original DIP models (as shown in Table 1 in their paper). Therefore, our LIP subnetworks achieve comparable performances with them.

Q5: There are also a number of works on designing losses for deep image prior so that the network will not be overfitted (e.g., Y Jo et al., Rethinking deep image prior for denoising, ICCV 2021).

[A]: Thanks for pointing that out. We have added relevant discussions to section 2.1 “Over-parameterized Image Priors”.

content.title: Thanks to AC and all reviewers. We would expect more engagement in the discussion.
content.comment:
Our sincere thanks to the AC and all reviewers’ efforts and constructive feedback, which helped us a lot in improving our work. We thank Reviewer fDwJ for appreciating the merits of our work. 

However, we regret that we are unable to engage the reviewers in the discussion period, even though we posted our response on Nov. 16 and followed up with a mild reminder on Nov. 18. While the reviewers have not replied or acknowledged that they have read our response, we hope that the reviewers could still take a close look at our responses before making the final assessment.

**Explanations of Our Method and Transferability Experiments**

We addressed this concern brought by Reviewer eUHy, bXEi, syh7 and fDwJ by adding detailed descriptions of IMP and generated masks in the appendix of the paper. We also move the algorithms and relevant descriptions to the main body of the paper. Also, we have added a comparison experiment in Fig.14 in Appendix B. We evaluate several single-image based LIP subnetworks (Baby-LIP, Bird-LIP, Woman-LIP and Butterfly-LIP) on the Baby.png and compare their performances with MUlti-LIP subnetworks. We found that when the sparsity level is low (0%-40%), the single-LIP subnetworks perform a little worse than the LIPs obtained on Baby.png. When the sparsity level increases (e.g., the number of remaining parameters is less than 0.6 million), they usually tend to perform comparably well. Another intriguing phenomenon is that Multi-LIP performs comparably with the LIPs obtained on Baby.png but can perform better than the other LIPs when the sparsity level is high, which also demonstrates that Multi-LIP could have better transferability than single-image based LIP subnetworks.

**Sparsity Level and Random Structure**

We addressed this concern brought by Reviewer eUHy and syh7 by first explaining how to compute the sparsity level based on pruning iterations. And then, we also refer the reviewers to our discussions on how to robustly stop the IMP loop (without requiring clean images as reference) while still identifying the matching subnetworks in Appendix B - “Discussions about the ‘early-stopping’ in the single-image based IMP loops”. Besides that, we have analyzed the inner structures of different LIP subnetworks in Section 4 “LIP in Untrained NNs” - paragraph “Why is the LIP Subnetwork Special and Good?”. And plot the layer-wise sparsity ratio of SNIP pruned, random pruned and LIP subnetworks in Fig. 7. Furthermore, we have added a new set of experiments: randomly prune the DIP model with the layer-wise sparsity ratio of the IMP method. In this way, we humbly draw our conjecture that LIP identifies non-trivial substructures and it is not trivial to find a “proper” random pruning scheme that will work. The results are summarized in Fig. 15 in Appendix B.

**Add more Relevant Works and A Stronger Baseline for Performance Comparisons**

We addressed this concern brought by Reviewer eUHy and bXEi. We first added the discussions of these relevant works in Section 2 BACKGROUND WORK of the paper. We further compare the LIP subnetworks with the “SynFlow” [a], one of the STOA pruning-at-initialization methods, in Table.4 in Appendix B.

[a] "Pruning neural networks without any data by iteratively conserving synaptic flow." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 6377-6389.

All of our revisions have been updated in the revised PDF file.

Best,

The Paper Authors

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn: This paper presents a method to prune the over-parameterized deep image prior (DIP) model by leveraging the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH). The proposed approach is shown to be capable of reducing the number of parameters in DIP while preserving the performance of the original DIP. Experiments are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method. This paper studies an important problem in deep learning and computer vision. After the rebuttal, all four reviewers have an agreement on rejecting the paper. The judgments are given below: Even though the proposed method is interesting, the novelty is insufficient, and common concerns about the motivation and practical application for this method remain. After reading the rebuttal and feedback from authors and reviewers, AC agrees with all reviewers that the current paper is not ready for publication, thus recommending rejecting the paper. AC urges the authors to improve their paper by taking into account all the suggestions provided by the reviewers, and then resubmit it to the next venue.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: Each of 4 reviewers rate the paper with a score of 5: marginal reject. They have common concerns on limited novelty, motivation and potential practical applications of the method.
